lesson.title: A neutral that carries more than the line

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the three lines' ripples fall into step and the neutral bar climb from 0 A past the 150 A line bar near a third, when you drag the third harmonic up.
interactive.title: Three line currents and their neutral
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A refresher lesson in eleven screens, with Back and Continue between them, on the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit whose loads draw harmonic currents. Screen 1, Do you still have it?: “A balanced three-phase load on a four-wire supply draws 60 A in each line. Its maker states a third harmonic of 35% of the line current. What current flows in the neutral?” Three choices, in this order: 0.00 A, 21.00 A, 63.00 A. Right: “Still there.”, the working 3 × 0.35 × 60 = 63.00 A,[^1] more than the 60 A in each line, so the neutral current, not the line current, sets the cable,[^2] and a line each on the slips: 0.00 A is true of the fundamentals alone, which cancel;[^3] 21.00 A is one line's third harmonic, 0.35 × 60, and the three lines' add;[^4] and 35% is row 3 of Table 4Aa: the neutral current, factor 0.86.[^13] Two buttons: Refresh the why (on to screen 2) and Skip to the practice (straight to screen 7). Wrong, 0.00 A: a balanced load's fundamentals do cancel in the neutral,[^3][^5] but third harmonic currents are additive there.[^4] Wrong, 21.00 A: that is one line's third harmonic; the neutral carries the sum of the three lines' third harmonic content,[^6] three times it. Then the right working and on to screen 2, with no skip. Read: the neutral carries 3 × 0.35 × 60 = 63.00 A, more than a line's 60 A. Screen 2, What it is for: a three-phase circuit is normally designed on its line current. Some circuits, supplying rectifiers, variable-speed motor drives or fluorescent lighting banks, draw currents that are not sinusoidal,[^7] and then the circuit may need designing on the neutral current, not the line current.[^2] The On-Site Guide asks the same of a discharge-lighting final circuit: it must carry its harmonic currents as well as the lamps' current.[^8] In red, if it is skipped: the neutral current gives rise to additional heating of the cables,[^9] and it comes without any matching fall in the line currents,[^10] so a cable sized on the line current alone does not allow for it. Screen 3, The why (why piece B): three line currents and their neutral. Opening text: each line current is drawn as two parts, a wave at the supply frequency (the fundamental) and a smaller wave at three times that frequency (the third harmonic). The picture: at the top, the three line currents, L1, L2 and L3, over one cycle of the supply; under them the neutral, their sum at each instant; under that two bars on one scale in amperes, Line and Neutral. A slider, Third harmonic, from 0 to 50% of the line current in steps of 1%, opening at 0%, with the edges of Table 4Aa's four rows as ticks under it, labelled 15, 33 and 45.[^11][^12][^13][^14] The line current is held at your slides' 150 A (p.35),[^1] so as the third harmonic's share grows the fundamental's shrinks. At 0% the three waves are plain sine waves a third of a cycle (120°) apart, and the neutral is flat at 0 A: balanced fundamentals cancel.[^3] Drag it up and each wave gains a ripple at three times the frequency. The 120° between the lines, marked by a bracket between L1's and L2's peaks (“120° = one ripple cycle”), is a whole cycle of that ripple, so the three ripples rise and fall together, in phase,[^15] and the neutral becomes a wave at three times the supply frequency, the sum of the three.[^6] On the first visit a short demonstration glides the slider from 0% to 35%; Replay runs it again, and coming back to the screen keeps his setting. Readouts: Neutral current, Ibn = 3 × h × IL;[^1] Current that sets the cable (the line's 150 A, or the neutral's once it is larger); Table 4Aa factor, by row. At 15%, 67.50 A; at 20%, 90.00 A; at 33%, 148.50 A; at 34%, 153.00 A, and the neutral bar passes the line bar and turns red; at 35%, 157.50 A; at 45%, 202.50 A, 135% of the line; at 50%, 225.00 A. On a row's edge (15, 33 or 45% exactly) the picture takes the lower row, as the IET's answer reads “exceeding 33 %”.[^16] One line under it: the other triple harmonics (the 9th, the 15th) add the same way;[^4] how high a real neutral goes depends on the load: a maker's note gives up to 173% of phase current,[^17] a paper up to three times the phase current at the fundamental frequency.[^18] Read: at 0% the neutral carries 0 A; it passes the 150 A line near a third, and at 35% carries 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A. Screen 4, Which current, which factor: the current tables are worked for three loaded conductors.[^19] A neutral carrying harmonic current is a fourth loaded conductor in the same cable or conduit: BS 7671 counts it as one where the third harmonic and its multiples pass 15% (Regulation 523.6.1, which NICEIC words as total harmonic distortion of the fundamental line current).[^20] Where a neutral carries only the lines' imbalance, its heat is offset by less heat in a line, and the cable is sized on the highest line current;[^21] harmonic current gets no such offset.[^10] Table 4Aa, as your slides give it (p.34), drawn as four rows stacked one above the other, each with its range, its current and its factor, and tapped to read its line: 0 to 15%, the line current with a factor of 1.0;[^11] 15 to 33%, the line current with 0.86;[^12] 33 to 45%, the neutral current with 0.86;[^13] over 45%, the neutral current with 1.0.[^14] Under the rows, why: up to 15% BS 7671 does not count the neutral as a loaded conductor, so the line current and a factor of 1.0 stand;[^20] up to 33% the line is still the larger, so it is Ib; above it the neutral is, and the cable is selected on the neutral current;[^22] the 0.86 is a rating factor, heat the table did not allow for (lesson 3),[^23] here the fourth loaded conductor's; by 45% the neutral carries 135% of the line, and with the cable sized on it the three lines are not fully loaded,[^24] so the factor goes back to 1.0. The factor goes in with the others: It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor).[^25] Before a device is chosen, the Schneider guide divides the current that sets the cable by the factor to give the design load it is chosen for.[^26] No neutral, no neutral current:[^30] a three-phase motor often has no neutral connected (p.33).[^5] Read: up to 33%, the line current sets the cable (factor 1.0 to 15%, 0.86 above); over 33%, the neutral current (0.86 to 45%, 1.0 above). Screen 5, Check: “A three-phase four-wire circuit carries 100 A in each line, and the maker's data gives a third harmonic of 50%. What current must its cable be chosen to carry, the current that sets it divided by Table 4Aa's factor?” Choices: 116.28 A, 150.00 A, 174.42 A. Right, 150.00 A: Ibn = 3 × 0.50 × 100 = 150.00 A, over 45%: the neutral current with a factor of 1.0.[^14] Wrong, 174.42 A (150.00 ÷ 0.86): the 0.86 belongs to the 33 to 45% row; above 45% the lines are not fully loaded.[^24] Wrong, 116.28 A (100 ÷ 0.86): that is the 15 to 33% row; at 50% the neutral carries 150% of the line, and the cable is selected on it.[^22] Read: 3 × 0.50 × 100 = 150.00 A, over 45%, factor 1.0: 150.00 A. Screen 6, Worked example, a line at each press (Work each step yourself first, then press Show), your slides p.35 and 36: a three-phase circuit with a harmonic content of 35% and a load of 150 A, single-core 70 °C thermoplastic cable on Reference Method B, grouped with three other circuits at an ambient of 35 °C, protected by a BS 88-2 fuse. 35% is row 3 of Table 4Aa, so the cable size is calculated on the neutral current.[^31] Ibn = 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A,[^1] more than 150 A, so Ibn is Ib.[^32] In: 160 A, from Fig 3A3(b).[^33] Ca 0.94 at 35 °C; Cg 0.65 for four circuits bunched;[^34] the factor 0.86.[^25] 0.94 × 0.65 = 0.611; 0.611 × 0.86 = 0.52546. It ≥ 160 ÷ 0.52546 = 304.50 A.[^25] Table 4D1A, column 5: 240 mm²,[^35] whose row in your copy (p.448) gives 346 A in that column.[^36] Iz = 346 × 0.52546 = 181.81 A, so 157.50 ≤ 160 ≤ 181.81. One line: your slides print 304.4 A, cut short; the cable is the same. Read: Ibn = 157.50 A is Ib; In 160 A; It ≥ 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) = 304.50 A; 240 mm², Iz 181.81 A. Screen 7, Section A, the course's question 3 (d): the showroom's scenario panel, and (a), (b) and (c) carried forward (4594 W; 8.22 A on L1; 160.44 A, the installation's maximum demand per phase). Given: DBL2's submain is fed three-phase and four-wire, as the course's split of its lighting circuits across L1 to L3 (lesson 2) needs, and most of its load is the key's fluorescent modular and twin fittings. The course takes their third harmonic as 20%, a practice value. Under it, the maker's figure: your slides consider harmonics only when the maker's data states one, and then its percentage goes into the sums;[^27][^28] no datasheet exists for the drawing's own fittings, and on the job no maker's figure means none is applied, so this part shows the method on a practice value. Makers often print total harmonic distortion, which counts every harmonic, not the third alone: a Thorn luminaire datasheet gives THD 15.00%;[^29] read which figure the datasheet gives, and say which you used. For scale, IEC 61000-3-2 limits the third harmonic of lighting equipment (Class C) to 30 × the circuit power factor, in percent.[^40][^41] The course applies the 20% to the whole of the heaviest line, L1, 8.22 A, though an LED circuit shares it: a cautious simplification, its own. “(d) Using your slides' rule and the heaviest line current, determine the neutral current of DBL2's submain.” A typed answer (part 3d): 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A.[^1] Slips: 1.64 A (0.20 × 8.22, one line's third harmonic: the three add[^6]), 0 A (the fundamentals cancel; the third harmonics do not[^4]), 24.66 A (3 × 8.22: the share h left out), 8.22 A (the line current). After two misses the working, and part (e) starts from the course's figure. Read: Ibn = 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A (on a practice 20%), less than the line's 8.22 A. Screen 8, Section A, question 3 (e): (a), (b), (c) and (d) carried forward. “(e) Determine the current DBL2's submain cable must be chosen to carry once Table 4Aa's factor is applied.” A typed answer (part 3e): 20% is the 15 to 33% row, the line current with 0.86,[^12] so 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A. Slips: 8.22 A (the factor left out: at 20% the neutral is a loaded conductor[^20]), 5.73 A (4.93 ÷ 0.86: the neutral is the smaller, and only above 33% does it set the cable[^16]), 7.07 A (8.22 × 0.86: rating factors divide[^37]). After it: 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A is what the Schneider guide calls the design load;[^26] once a device is chosen, In takes Ib's place in It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × 0.86),[^25] as lesson 8 does for this submain, so 9.56 A is a floor, not the It the cable is finally chosen on. Then a what-if: if the maker's figure were 35% (the slides' example percentage, not a showroom figure), 3 × 0.35 × 8.22 = 8.63 A, more than 8.22 A, so the neutral would set the cable: 8.63 ÷ 0.86 = 10.03 A. Read: 20% is the 15 to 33% row: 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A (on a practice 20%). Screen 9, Section B: “Explain why third harmonic currents add in the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit, and what that means for the cable.” Your written answer, marked against four points (a full answer makes any three, so at least one says what it means for the cable), one more go, then the model answer. Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers: “A three-phase four-wire circuit carries 37 A in each line, and the maker's data gives a third harmonic of 40%. Determine the current its cable must be chosen to carry once Table 4Aa's factor is applied.” A typed answer: 3 × 0.40 × 37 = 44.40 A, more than 37 A, so the 33 to 45% row: 44.40 ÷ 0.86 = 51.63 A; the Schneider guide works the same circuit and prints 51.6 A.[^26] Slips: 44.40 A (the 0.86 left out), 43.02 A (37 ÷ 0.86: the line current, but over 33% the neutral sets the cable), 38.18 A (44.40 × 0.86: the factor divides). Read: 3 × 0.40 × 37 = 44.40 A; 44.40 ÷ 0.86 = 51.63 A. Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson. The line under the lesson (figures from your slides, your assignment and your copy of BS 7671; practice values marked; each line worked from the rounded figures before it) shows on screens 3 to 8 and 10.
interactive.ignores: Each line current is drawn as a fundamental and a third harmonic only; real loads also draw the 5th, 7th and higher harmonics, and of those only the triple ones (9th, 15th) add in the neutral. The three lines are drawn equal; real ones differ a little, and the neutral then also carries a small part of the fundamentals. Where the ripple sits against the fundamental is chosen for the drawing: the size of each part, not the shape of the wave, sets the readouts. Table 4Aa's rows are steps, so a figure just across an edge changes the factor at once.

explain.text:
In a balanced three-phase circuit drawing plain sine-wave currents, the three line currents cancel in the neutral, so a balanced motor may have no neutral connected at all.[^3][^5] Some loads, such as fluorescent lighting banks, rectifiers and variable-speed drives, draw currents that are not sinusoidal,[^7] and part of what they draw does not cancel: the third harmonics of the three lines add in the neutral,[^4] and can make it carry more than any line.[^38] Then the neutral current, not the line current, may have to set the cable.[^2]

Picture each line current as two waves added together: one at the supply frequency, the fundamental, and a smaller one at three times that frequency, the [[third harmonic]]. The three fundamentals of a balanced load are a third of a cycle, 120°, apart, so at every instant they sum to nothing in the neutral.[^3] The third harmonic runs three times as fast, so that same 120° delay is a whole cycle of it: the three lines' third harmonics rise and fall together, in phase,[^15] and the neutral carries their sum.[^6] If each line's third harmonic is a share h of its line current IL, the neutral carries Ibn = 3 × h × IL.[^1] That passes IL once 3h passes 1, near a third: your slides' 150 A load at 35% puts 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A in the neutral.[^1] This is a simplified picture, three equal lines and the third harmonic alone; the other triple harmonics add in the same way.[^4]

The current tables are worked for three loaded conductors,[^19] and a neutral carrying harmonic current is a fourth [[loaded conductor]] heating the same cable or conduit;[^9] BS 7671 counts it as one once the third harmonic and its multiples pass 15% of the fundamental line current (in NICEIC's summary of Regulation 523.6.1).[^20] More heat in the same cable means each conductor reaches its limit at a lower current, so the cable is derated: that is Table 4Aa's 0.86. A neutral that carries only the lines' imbalance is offset by less heat in a line;[^21] a harmonic neutral current comes with no such fall in the lines.[^10] So Table 4Aa, as your slides give it, picks the current and a rating factor by the third harmonic: up to 15%, the line current with 1.0;[^11] 15 to 33%, the line current with 0.86;[^12] 33 to 45%, the neutral current with 0.86;[^13] over 45%, the neutral current with 1.0,[^14] because by then the neutral carries over 135% of the line and the three lines are not fully loaded.[^24] The factor divides In with the others: It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor).[^25] Your slides start all of this from the maker's data: harmonics are considered only when it says one is present, and its percentage goes into the sums (p.37).[^27][^28]

**Where the maker's data gives a third harmonic of more than about a third of the line current, the neutral carries more than the line, and the neutral current, Ibn = 3 × h × IL, sets the cable.**[^2][^1][^13]

analogy.text: Picture three watches on a ship whose days start eight hours apart. Anything each watch does once in its own day, such as taking over, falls at three different times, spread evenly round the clock. But anything each watch does every eight hours of its own day falls at the same times for all three, because an eight-hour stagger is a whole lap of an eight-hour routine: at those times the galley serves all three watches at once, three times one watch's queue.
analogy.breaks: People spread out but never subtract, while the fundamentals, being signed currents, cancel to nothing. And how big each line's third harmonic is comes from the load's electronics, not a rota: the picture shows why they line up, not how large they are.

practice.text:
- Ask for the maker's data on each load that draws non-sinusoidal current: fluorescent fittings with their control gear, rectifiers, variable-speed drives.[^7] Your slides consider harmonics only if it says one will be present, and then its percentage goes into the sums (p.37).[^27][^28] Note whether it gives the third harmonic or THD.[^29]
- Work the neutral current with the heaviest line current: Ibn = 3 × h × IL.[^1]
- Read Table 4Aa's row: up to 15%, the line current with 1.0;[^11] 15 to 33%, the line current with 0.86;[^12] 33 to 45%, the neutral current with 0.86;[^13] over 45%, the neutral current with 1.0.[^14]
- Choose In from that current, then It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor),[^25] and read Table 4D1A's column for three or four cables, three-phase a.c.[^35]
- Check Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, with Iz worked from the same factors.[^39]

**Rule of thumb:** the neutral overtakes the line near a third, where 3 × h passes 1. A circuit with no neutral carries no neutral current,[^30] so a three-phase motor's cable without one has no neutral to size.[^5]

**Worked example:** your slides' 150 A circuit at 35% (p.35, 36). Ibn = 3 × 0.35 × 150 = 157.50 A, more than 150 A, so it is Ib.[^1][^32] In 160 A.[^33] It ≥ 160 ÷ (0.94 × 0.65 × 0.86) = 160 ÷ 0.52546 = 304.50 A (your slides print 304.4 A, cut short).[^25] Table 4D1A column 5: 240 mm² at 346 A,[^35][^36] so Iz = 346 × 0.52546 = 181.81 A and 157.50 ≤ 160 ≤ 181.81. On the showroom, with a third harmonic of 20% (a practice value: read the real one from the maker's datasheet), DBL2's submain has Ibn = 3 × 0.20 × 8.22 = 4.93 A, below the line's 8.22 A, so the line current sets it: 8.22 ÷ 0.86 = 9.56 A.

**Common mistakes**
- Expecting no neutral current because the load is balanced: true of the fundamentals only.[^3][^4]
- Leaving out the × 3: h × IL is one line's third harmonic, and the neutral carries all three.[^6]
- Sizing on the line current when the third harmonic exceeds 33%.[^16]
- Leaving out the 0.86 between 15 and 45%, or keeping it above 45%.[^12][^13][^14]
- Reading a THD figure as the third harmonic without saying so.[^20]

b1.q: Explain why third harmonic currents add in the neutral of a three-phase four-wire circuit, and what that means for the cable.

points.text: The fundamental currents of a balanced load are 120° apart and cancel in the neutral, but the third harmonics of the three lines are in phase (a 120° shift is a whole cycle of a wave three times as fast), so they do not cancel.
points.cite: Slides p.33; Wired IN (Federal Pacific), Mar-Apr 2007, in research; Schneider Electrical Installation Guide, sizing the neutral conductor, Fig. G64, in research; IJEAT paper on triplen harmonics, in research

points.text: They add: the neutral carries the sum of the three lines' third harmonic content, Ibn = 3 × h × IL.
points.cite: IET Wiring Matters 62 (Autumn 2016), in research; slides p.35

points.text: Above about a third (33%) of the line current the neutral current is the larger, so the cable is sized on the neutral current.
points.cite: Slides p.34 to 36; IET EngX answer on Table 4Aa, in research

points.text: The neutral becomes a loaded conductor that heats the cable, which the tables (three loaded conductors) do not allow for, so Table 4Aa applies a factor of 0.86 between 15% and 45%.
points.cite: IET Wiring Matters 23 (Summer 2007); NICEIC on Regulation 523.6.1; Schneider guide, in research; slides p.34

b1.model: In a balanced load the three fundamental currents are 120° apart, so they cancel in the neutral (your slides p.33). The third harmonic runs at three times the supply frequency, so the same 120° between the lines is a whole cycle of it: the three lines' third harmonics are in phase and do not cancel. They add, and the neutral carries the sum of the three lines' third harmonic content, 3 × h × IL (slides p.35). Above about a third of the line current that is more than the line current, so the cable is sized on the neutral current (Table 4Aa, slides p.34 to 36). Above 15% the neutral is also a fourth loaded conductor heating the cable, which the current tables, worked for three, do not allow for, so Table 4Aa applies a factor of 0.86 between 15% and 45%.

summary.title: A neutral that carries more than the line
summary.for: Loads such as fluorescent lighting banks, rectifiers and drives draw non-sinusoidal current; the three lines' third harmonics add in the neutral, which can then carry more than a line. Table 4Aa says which current sets the cable and by what factor (slides p.33, 34).
summary.rule:
Ibn = 3 × h × IL (h: the third harmonic as a share of the line current)
0 to 15%: line current, factor 1.0
15 to 33%: line current, factor 0.86
33 to 45%: neutral current, factor 0.86
over 45%: neutral current, factor 1.0
It ≥ In ÷ (Ca × Cg × the Table 4Aa factor)

Only when the maker's data gives a harmonic figure (slides p.37); say whether it is the third harmonic or THD.
Balanced fundamentals cancel in the neutral; third harmonics add.
No neutral, no neutral current.

traps.text: Expecting no neutral current from a balanced load: true of the fundamentals only.

traps.text: Leaving out the × 3: h × IL is one line's third harmonic.
traps.cite: Slides p.35; IET Wiring Matters 62 (Autumn 2016), in research

traps.text: Sizing on the line current above 33%: at 35% your slides' 150 A circuit has 157.50 A in the neutral.
Leaving out the 0.86 between 15 and 45%, or keeping it above 45%.
Reading a datasheet's THD as the third harmonic without saying so.

interactive.title: Three line currents and their neutral
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the three lines' ripples fall into step and the neutral bar climb from 0 A past the 150 A line bar near a third, when you drag the third harmonic up.

checks.label: At 0% the 120° shift makes the three line currents cancel in the neutral at every instant
The neutral's current equals the sum of the three lines' third harmonic content: at 35%, 3 × 52.50 = 157.50 A
Each line stays at 150 A as the third harmonic grows: the fundamental shrinks to make room
The neutral rises at every step and passes the 150 A line between 33% and 34%
Table 4Aa's rows: 15% row 1, 16% and 33% row 2 on the line, 34% and 45% row 3 on the neutral, 46% row 4
If the neutral current is more than 135% of the phase current the phases are not fully loaded: 45% gives exactly 135%
37 A at 40% third harmonic: neutral 37 × 0.4 × 3 = 44.4 A, design load 44.4 ÷ 0.86 = 51.6 A
The recall and check: 63.00, 0.00 and 21.00 A; 150.00, 174.42 and 116.28 A, as the case file works them
The worked example: 0.611 and 0.52546, It 304.50 A, Iz 181.81 A, as the case file works it
The demonstration opens at 0% and settles on your slides' 35%
Every slip lies outside its answer's accepted range

applied.problem: Screen 7: DBL2 has 22 fluorescent fittings of 83 (case file), so they are most of its load (3056 of 4594 W), not most fittings. Screen 4: the Schneider guide sizes the cable on the design load, not a device. A single-core neutral shares a conduit, not a cable.

The opening says a balanced three-phase circuit's line currents cancel in the neutral, which read alone on a review card is false for the harmonic loads the lesson is about; its source (Wired IN) says this of linear loads' balanced portions. Also a single-core neutral (the slides' example) heats th…

"Either way the neutral is now a fourth loaded conductor" covers every percentage below a third, but the slides' Table 4Aa takes factor 1.0 up to 15% and NICEIC's 523.6.1 counts the neutral as loaded only above 15%.
